chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: Some things are within our power, and some things are not. Within our power are our opinions, intentions, desires, aversions — in a word, whatever belongs to us. Beyond our power are our body, property, reputation, public office — in a word, whatever is not truly ours.

The things within our power are by nature free, unrestricted, unhindered; the things beyond our power are weak, dependent, restricted, and foreign. Remember, then, that if you treat what is naturally dependent as if it were free, and take what belongs to others as your own, you will be obstructed, you will grieve, you will be disturbed, and you will blame both gods and men. But if you claim as your own only what is actually your own, and see what belongs to others for what it really is, then no one will ever compel you, no one will restrict you; you will blame no one, accuse no one, do nothing against your will; no one will harm you, you will have no enemy, and you will suffer no injury.

Since you are aiming at such great things, remember that you must not allow yourself even the slightest inclination toward the others; you must give some up entirely and postpone the rest for now. If you want both these things and also wealth and power, you may fail to gain the latter while pursuing the former, and you will certainly lose the one thing by which happiness and freedom are secured.

Train yourself, then, to say to every harsh impression, “You are only an impression and not at all what you appear to be.” Then examine it by the rules you have — above all, by this one: whether it concerns things within our power or things beyond it. And if it concerns something beyond our power, be ready to say that it is nothing to you.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Remember that desire demands getting what you want, and aversion demands avoiding what you do not want. Whoever fails to get what he desires is disappointed, and whoever meets with what he is averse to is miserable. So if you avoid only the things within your control that you do not want, you will never encounter what you shun; but if you try to avoid sickness, death, or poverty, you risk misery. Take aversion, then, away from everything that is not in our power, and apply it to the undesirable things that are. But for now, suppress desire altogether — for if you desire anything beyond our power, you will necessarily be disappointed, and even the things within our power that deserve to be desired are not yet secure for you. Where practical necessity forces you to pursue or avoid something, do even this with care, gentleness, and moderation.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: With regard to anything that delights the mind, serves a use, or is dearly loved, remind yourself of its nature — beginning with the smallest things. If you are fond of a cup, say to yourself, “It is a cup I am fond of,” so that when it breaks, you can bear it. When you embrace your child or your wife, remember that you embrace a mortal — and so, if either should die, you can bear it.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: When you are about to begin any action, remind yourself of its nature. If you are going to the baths, picture what usually happens there — some splashing water about, some pushing past, others shouting, others stealing. You will go about it more safely if you say to yourself, “I am going to bathe, and I will keep my will in harmony with nature.” Do the same with every other action. Then, if anything hinders your bathing, you can say, “It was not only to bathe that I wanted, but also to keep my will in harmony with nature — and I shall not do that if I grow upset at what happens.”

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: People are disturbed not by things, but by the views they take of them. Death, for instance, is nothing terrible — otherwise it would have seemed so to Socrates. The terror lies in our notion that death is terrible. So whenever we are hindered, disturbed, or grieved, let us never blame others, but ourselves — that is, our own views. It is the mark of an uneducated person to reproach others for his own misfortunes; of one beginning to learn, to reproach himself; and of one fully educated, to reproach neither others nor himself.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Do not be proud of any excellence that is not your own. If a horse in its pride said, “I am handsome,” that might be tolerable. But when you boast, “I have a handsome horse,” know that you are proud only of the horse's merit. What, then, is your own? The use you make of your impressions. So when you are in harmony with nature in that use, you will have reason for pride — for you will be proud of a good that is truly your own.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Imagine a voyage: the ship is at anchor, and you go ashore to fetch water. You may amuse yourself along the way by picking up a shellfish or a truffle, but your thoughts should stay fixed on the ship and be constantly alert, in case the captain calls. Then you must leave all these things behind, or be carried on board bound like a sheep. So too in life: if, instead of a shellfish or a truffle, you are given a wife or a child, there is no harm in that. But if the captain calls, run to the ship, leave everything, and do not look back. And if you are old, never go far from the ship, so that you are not missing when called.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Do not demand that events happen as you wish; wish instead that they happen as they do — and you will get on well.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Sickness is a hindrance to the body, but not to the will — unless the will chooses to be hindered. Lameness hinders the leg, but not the will. Say this to yourself about everything that happens, and you will find that it is a hindrance to something else, but not truly to you.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: Whenever something happens to you, remember to turn to yourself and ask what faculty you have for dealing with it. If you meet a handsome person, you will find that the faculty needed is self-restraint; if pain, endurance; if insult, patience. Train yourself in this habit, and the events of life will not overwhelm you.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: Never say of anything, “I have lost it,” but rather, “I have given it back.” Has your child died? He has been given back. Has your wife died? She has been given back. Has your estate been taken? That too has been given back. “But the one who took it was a bad man.” What does it matter to you by whose hands the giver has asked for it back? For as long as he allows you to have it, treat it as something that is not your own — as travelers treat their lodging at an inn.

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: If you want to make progress, give up such reasoning as, “If I neglect my affairs, I will have no livelihood,” or, “If I do not punish my servant, he will be good for nothing.” It is better to die of hunger free from grief and fear than to live in abundance with inner turmoil; and it is better that your servant should be bad than that you should be unhappy.

Begin, then, with little things. Is a little oil spilled or a little wine stolen? Say to yourself, “This is the price of peace and tranquillity — and nothing is had for nothing.” When you call your servant, consider that he may not come when you call, or, if he does, may not do what you wish. It is not at all good for him, and very bad for you, if he has the power to disturb your peace.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: If you want to make progress, be content to be thought foolish and dull in regard to externals. Do not wish to be thought knowledgeable; and even if you seem to others to be someone of consequence, distrust yourself. Know this: it is not easy both to keep your will in harmony with nature and to secure external things. While you are absorbed in one, you must inevitably neglect the other.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: If you wish your children, your wife, and your friends to live forever, you are foolish — for you are wishing things to be in your power that are not, and what belongs to others to be your own. So too, if you wish your servant to be without fault, you are foolish; you are wishing vice not to be vice but something else. But if you wish not to be disappointed in your desires, that is in your power. Train yourself, then, in what is in your power. A man's master is whoever is able to give or take away what that man seeks or shuns. Whoever wants to be free, then, must neither desire nor reject anything that depends on others; otherwise he will inevitably be a slave.

chapters.title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: Remember that you must behave in life as at a banquet. Is something brought your way? Reach out and take a moderate portion. Does it pass you by? Do not stop it. Has it not yet come? Do not stretch out in longing; wait until it reaches you. Do the same with children, wife, public office, and wealth — and in time you will be worthy to feast with the gods. And if you go so far as not even to take what is set before you, but can do without it, then you will not only be worthy to feast with the gods, but to rule with them as well. It was by acting this way that Diogenes, Heraclitus, and others like them deservedly became divine, and were recognized as such.

chapters.title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: When you see someone weeping in grief — because his son has gone abroad or because he has suffered a loss in his affairs — take care not to be carried away by the appearance of evil. Instead, distinguish clearly and be ready to say, “What hurts this man is not the event itself, for another would not be hurt by it, but the view he has chosen to take of it.” As far as conversation goes, though, do not refuse to adapt to him, and if need be, to sigh along with him. Only take care not to sigh inwardly as well.

chapters.title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: Remember that you are an actor in a play, whose nature is determined by the Author — if short, in a short one; if long, in a long one. If it is his pleasure that you should play a poor man, a cripple, a ruler, or a private citizen, see that you play it well. For this is your business: to act your given part well. To choose it belongs to another.

chapters.title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: When a raven happens to croak ominously, do not be carried away by the appearance, but distinguish and say, “Nothing is foretold to me — not to my paltry body, nor my property, nor reputation, nor children, nor wife. To me all omens are favorable if I will it so. For whatever happens, it is in my power to draw benefit from it.”

chapters.title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: You can be invincible if you never enter a contest in which it is not in your power to win. When you see someone exalted by honors, power, or great esteem of any kind, take care not to be dazzled by appearances and to pronounce him happy. For if the essence of good lies in things within our own power, there is no room for envy or rivalry. As for you, do not desire to be a general, a senator, or a consul — desire instead to be free; and the only road to freedom is to disregard the things that are not within our power.

chapters.title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Remember that it is not the one who abuses or strikes you who insults you, but your view that these things are insulting. So when someone provokes you, know that it is your own judgment that has provoked you. Try, then, first of all, not to be carried away by appearances. For if you once gain time and breathing room, you will more easily master yourself.

chapters.title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: Keep death, exile, and everything else that seems terrible daily before your eyes — above all, death. Then you will never entertain a base thought or crave anything too eagerly.

chapters.title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: If you have a serious desire for philosophy, prepare yourself from the very start to have the crowd laugh and sneer at you, and say, “He has come back to us a philosopher all at once,” and, “Where did he get this haughty look?” As for you, do not wear a haughty look, but hold steadily to the things that seem best to you, as one appointed by God to this particular station. Remember: if you persist, the very people who first ridiculed you will afterwards admire you. But if you are defeated by them, you will draw a double ridicule.

chapters.title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: If you ever turn your attention to externals in order to please someone, know that you have ruined your whole plan of life. Be content, then, in everything, with being a philosopher; and if you wish also to appear one, appear so to yourself — and that will be enough.

chapters.title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: Do not let thoughts like these distress you: “I shall live in disgrace and be nobody anywhere.” If disgrace is an evil, you can no more be drawn into evil through another than into baseness. Is it your business, then, to gain power or to be invited to a banquet? Not at all. How, then, is this a disgrace? And how is it true that you will be nobody anywhere, when you ought to be somebody only in those things that are within your own power, where you may be of the greatest account? “But my friends will go unassisted.” What do you mean by “unassisted”? They will not have money from you, nor will you make them Roman citizens. Who told you, then, that these belong to the things within our power, rather than to the affairs of others? And who can give to another what he does not himself possess? “Well, then, acquire these things so that we too may have a share.” If I can acquire them while preserving my honor, fidelity, and self-respect, show me the way, and I will do so. But if you require me to lose my own proper good, so that you may gain what is no real good, see how unreasonable and foolish you are. Besides, which would you rather have — a sum of money or a loyal and honorable friend? Help me, then, to keep this character, rather than asking me to do the things that would destroy it. “But my country,” you say, “as far as depends on me, will go unassisted.” Again, what sort of assistance do you mean? It will not get porticoes or baths from you. And what of that? Neither does a smith supply it with shoes, nor a shoemaker with weapons. It is enough that each fully performs his own proper work. If you were to supply it with another faithful and honorable citizen, would he not be of use to it? Yes. Then neither are you useless to it. “What place, then,” you ask, “shall I hold in the state?” Whatever place you can hold while preserving your honor and fidelity. But if, by wanting to be useful to the state, you lose these qualities, how can you serve your country once you have become faithless and shameless?

chapters.title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: Is someone preferred to you at a banquet, in courtesies, or in private counsel? If these things are good, you should rejoice that he has them; and if they are bad, do not grieve that you do not. Remember that you cannot rival others for externals without using the same means they use to obtain them. How can the man who will not haunt another's door, will not attend him, will not praise him, have an equal share with the man who does these things? You are unjust and unreasonable, then, if you are unwilling to pay the price at which these things are sold, yet want to have them for nothing. How much is a head of lettuce sold for? An obol, for instance. If another man pays an obol and takes the lettuces, while you, not paying, go without, do not think he has gained an advantage over you. He has the lettuces; you have the obol you did not give. In the same way, you were not invited to such-and-such a person's banquet because you did not pay him the price at which a supper is sold. It is sold for praise; it is sold for attendance. Pay him the price, then, if it is to your advantage. But if you wish to keep the one and receive the other, you are unreasonable and foolish. Have you nothing, then, in place of the supper? Yes, indeed — you have the freedom of not praising someone you do not wish to praise, and of not having to endure the insolence of his lackeys.

chapters.title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: The will of nature can be learned from things on which we all agree. When our neighbor's boy breaks a cup or the like, we are quick to say, “These things happen.” Know, then, that when your own cup is broken, you ought to be affected exactly as you were when another's cup was broken. Apply this to greater things. Has the child or wife of another died? No one would fail to say, “It is the common lot of mortals.” But when a man's own child dies, immediately the cry is, “Alas, how wretched I am!” We should always remember how we are affected when we hear the same thing about others.

chapters.title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: As a target is not set up for the sake of missing the mark, so neither does the nature of evil exist in the world.

chapters.title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: If someone handed over your body to any passerby, you would certainly be angry. Do you feel no shame, then, in handing over your own mind to anyone who reviles you, letting it be disturbed and confounded?
XXIX

In every undertaking, consider what comes before it and what follows, and only then begin. Otherwise you will start with enthusiasm, careless of the consequences, and when these emerge, you will shamefully give up. “I would win the Olympic Games.” But consider what precedes and what follows, and then, if it is to your advantage, engage in it. You must conform to rules, submit to a diet, refrain from delicacies; exercise your body, whether you feel like it or not, at set hours, in heat and cold; you must drink no cold water, and sometimes no wine — in a word, you must give yourself over to your trainer as to a physician. Then, in the contest, you may be flung into a ditch, dislocate your arm, twist your ankle, swallow quantities of dust, be flogged for negligence, and, after all that, lose the victory. When you have reckoned up all this, if your inclination still holds, set about the contest. Otherwise, you will behave like children, who sometimes play at being wrestlers, sometimes gladiators, sometimes trumpeters, sometimes tragic actors, whenever they have seen and admired these shows. So you too will be at one moment a wrestler, at another a gladiator; now a philosopher, now an orator — but nothing in earnest. Like an ape, you imitate whatever you see, and one thing after another pleases you, but falls out of favor as soon as it becomes familiar. For you have never entered on anything with consideration, nor after surveying and testing the whole matter, but carelessly and with half-hearted zeal. So some, when they have seen a philosopher, or heard a man speaking like Euphrates — though who, indeed, can speak like him? — decide they want to be philosophers too. Consider first, my friend, what the matter is, and what your own nature is able to bear. If you wish to be a wrestler, consider your shoulders, your back, your thighs; for different people are made for different things. Do you think you can go on acting as you do now and be a philosopher — that you can eat, drink, grow angry, be discontented, just as you are now? You must keep vigil, you must labor, you must master certain appetites; you must leave your acquaintances, be despised by your servant, laughed at by those you meet; come off worse than others in everything — in offices, honors, and before tribunals. When you have fully considered all this, approach, if you still wish — that is, if by giving these up you wish to purchase serenity, freedom, and tranquillity. If not, do not come here; do not, like children, be now a philosopher, then a tax-collector, then an orator, and then one of Caesar's officers. These roles are not consistent with one another. You must be one man, either good or bad. You must cultivate either your own reason or externals; apply yourself either to what is within or to what is outside you — that is, be either a philosopher or one of the mob.

chapters.title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: Duties are universally measured by our relationships. Is a certain man your father? Then this implies caring for him, yielding to him in all things, bearing his reproaches and his corrections patiently. “But he is a bad father.” Is your natural bond, then, to a good father? No — to a father. “My brother is unjust.” Well, preserve your own just relation toward him. Do not consider what he does, but what you must do to keep your own will in harmony with nature. Another cannot hurt you unless you please; you will be hurt when you consent to be hurt. In this way, if you habituate yourself to contemplating the relations of neighbor, citizen, commander, you can deduce from each the corresponding duties.

chapters.title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: Know that the essence of piety toward the gods lies in this: to form right opinions concerning them — that they exist, and that they govern the universe justly and well. Fix yourself in the resolve to obey them, to yield to them, and willingly to follow them through all events, as being ruled by the most perfect wisdom. In this way you will never find fault with the gods, nor accuse them of neglecting you. This can be achieved in no other way than by withdrawing yourself from things that are not in our power, and by making good and evil consist only in those that are. For if you suppose anything else to be good or evil, it is inevitable that, when you are disappointed of what you wish or encounter what you would avoid, you will reproach and blame those responsible. Every creature is naturally formed to flee and loathe what appears harmful, together with its cause, and to pursue and admire what appears beneficial, together with its cause. It is impossible, then, for one who supposes himself harmed to rejoice in the person who (as he thinks) harmed him, just as it is impossible to rejoice in the harm itself. Hence also a father is reviled by his son when he does not give him what seems good; and this made Polynices and Eteocles enemies to each other — for empire seemed good to both. It is for this reason that the farmer reviles the gods, and so do the sailor, the merchant, and those who have lost wife or child. Where our interest lies, there, too, is our piety directed. So whoever is careful to regulate his desires and aversions rightly is thereby also made careful of piety. It becomes everyone's duty, moreover, to offer libations and sacrifices and first fruits according to the customs of his country, doing so purely, and not carelessly or negligently, nor stingily, nor yet extravagantly.

chapters.title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: When you consult a diviner, remember that you do not know what the event will be, and you come to learn it from the diviner; but as to its nature, you knew that before coming — at least, if you are of philosophical mind. For if it belongs to the things not within our own power, it cannot possibly be either good or evil. Do not, then, bring with you to the diviner either desire or aversion — otherwise you will approach him trembling. Understand first, clearly, that every event is indifferent and nothing to you, whatever sort it may be, for it will be in your power to make a right use of it, and no one can prevent this. Then come with confidence to the gods as your counselors; and afterwards, when any counsel has been given, remember what counselors you have chosen, and whose advice you will be neglecting if you disobey. Approach divination as Socrates prescribed, in cases whose whole concern is the outcome, and where neither reason nor any other art provides the means to discover what is at issue. When, therefore, it is our duty to share in the danger of a friend or of our country, we must not consult the oracle on whether to share it with them. Even if the diviner forewarns you that the auspices are unfavorable, this means no more than that death, mutilation, or exile is foretold. But reason within us bids us, even with these hazards, to stand by our friend and our country. Attend, then, to the greater diviner, the Pythian God, who once cast out of the temple the man who neglected to save his friend.

chapters.title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: Begin by prescribing to yourself a certain character and bearing, such as you may maintain both alone and in company.

Be mostly silent, or say only what is needful, and in few words. We may, however, enter sparingly into conversation when occasion requires, but not on common topics — gladiators, horse races, athletic champions, food, or drink, the vulgar subjects of talk — and especially not on people, by blaming, praising, or comparing them. If you are able, bring the conversation of your company around to proper subjects by your own talk; but if you find yourself among strangers, be silent.
Let your laughter not be loud, frequent, or abundant.
Avoid taking oaths, if possible, altogether; or at least as far as you are able.

Avoid public and vulgar entertainments; but if an occasion calls you to them, keep your attention stretched taut, lest you slide imperceptibly into vulgarity. Know that even if a person is himself quite pure, if his companion is corrupted, the one who keeps company with him will be corrupted too.
Provide things relating to the body no further than absolute need requires — food, drink, clothing, house, attendants. But cut off everything that tends toward display and luxury.

Before marriage, guard yourself with all your strength from unlawful relations with women; yet be not uncharitable or severe toward those who give in to them, nor constantly boast that you yourself do otherwise.

If anyone tells you that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make excuses about what is said, but answer, “He was ignorant of my other faults, otherwise he would not have mentioned only these.”

It is not necessary for you to appear often at public spectacles; but if an occasion does call for it, show no more concern for anyone than for yourself — that is, wish things to be just as they are, and only the best man to win; then nothing will go against you. Abstain entirely from shouting, mockery, and violent emotion. And when you leave, do not talk much about what happened, unless it contributes to your own improvement. Such talk would show that you were dazzled by the spectacle.
Do not be quick or eager to attend private recitations; but if you do attend, maintain your gravity and dignity, yet avoid being disagreeable.

When you are about to meet with anyone, and especially with someone who seems your superior, picture to yourself how Socrates or Zeno would conduct himself in such a case, and you will not be at a loss to handle whatever happens properly.

When you are about to go before a person in power, imagine that you may not find him at home, that you may be shut out, that the doors may not be opened, that he may not notice you. If, despite all this, it is your duty to go, bear what happens and never say, “It was not worth so much”; that is vulgar, and the mark of a man overwhelmed by externals.

In company, avoid frequent and excessive mention of your own actions and dangers. However agreeable it is to you to recall the risks you have run, it is not equally agreeable to others to hear your adventures. Avoid, likewise, any attempt to provoke laughter, for this can easily drag you into vulgarity, and is apt to lower you in the esteem of your acquaintances. Approaches to indecent talk are dangerous too. Therefore, when anything of this sort arises, take the first fitting opportunity to rebuke the one making such advances; or at least, by silence, blushing, and a serious look, show that you are displeased with such talk.

chapters.title: Chapter 33
paragraphs: If you are dazzled by the appearance of some promised pleasure, guard yourself against being carried away by it; let the matter wait your leisure, and allow yourself a delay. Then bring to mind both moments in time — the one in which you will enjoy the pleasure, and the one in which, afterward, you will repent and reproach yourself — and set against these how glad and self-approving you will be if you abstain. Even if it seems a fitting indulgence, take care that its enticements, allurements, and seductions do not overcome you, and set against them how much better it is to be conscious of having won so great a victory.

chapters.title: Chapter 34
paragraphs: When you do anything from a clear judgment that it ought to be done, never shrink from being seen to do it, even if the world should misunderstand it. If you are not acting rightly, avoid the action itself; if you are, why fear those who wrongly censure you?

chapters.title: Chapter 35
paragraphs: As the proposition, “It is either day or night,” has great force in a disjunctive argument but none at all in a conjunctive one, so at a feast to take the largest share suits the bodily appetite well enough but is utterly at odds with the social spirit of the meal. When you eat with another, remember not only the value to the body of what is set before you, but also the value of proper courtesy toward your host.

chapters.title: Chapter 36
paragraphs: If you have taken on any role beyond your strength, you have both conducted yourself poorly in it and abandoned one you could have carried well.

chapters.title: Chapter 37
paragraphs: As in walking you take care not to step on a nail or twist your foot, so likewise take care not to injure the ruling faculty of your mind. If we guarded against this in every action, we would enter upon action more safely.

chapters.title: Chapter 38
paragraphs: The body is the proper measure of each person's possessions, as the foot is the measure of the shoe. If you stop at this, you will keep the measure; but if you go beyond it, you must necessarily be carried forward as down a cliff. It is the same with a shoe: once you go beyond its fitness to the foot, it comes first to be gilded, then purple, and then studded with jewels. For what once exceeds the proper measure knows no limit.

chapters.title: Chapter 39
paragraphs: Women from the age of fourteen are flattered by men with the title of mistresses. Perceiving that they are regarded as qualified only to give men pleasure, they begin to adorn themselves, and place all their hopes in that. It is worth the effort, then, to make them perceive that they are honored only insofar as they appear beautiful in their bearing and modestly virtuous.

chapters.title: Chapter 40
paragraphs: It is a mark of want of intellect to spend much time on matters of the body — as to be immoderate in exercise, eating, drinking, and the other animal functions. These things should be done in passing; our main strength should be given to our reason.

chapters.title: Chapter 41
paragraphs: When anyone treats you ill or speaks ill of you, remember that he acts or speaks from the impression that it is right for him to do so. It is impossible for him to follow what appears right to you, but only what appears so to himself. Therefore, if his judgment is based on false appearances, he is the one hurt, since he is the one deceived. For if anyone takes a true proposition to be false, the proposition is not harmed, only the man is deceived. Starting from these principles, you will bear meekly with a person who reviles you; for on every occasion you will say, “It seemed so to him.”

chapters.title: Chapter 42
paragraphs: Everything has two handles: one by which it can be carried, another by which it cannot. If your brother acts unjustly, do not grasp the matter by the handle of his injustice, for by that it cannot be borne. Rather grasp it by the opposite — that he is your brother, that he was brought up with you — and so you will take hold of it as it can be borne.

chapters.title: Chapter 43
paragraphs: These reasonings have no logical connection: “I am richer than you, therefore I am your superior.” “I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am your superior.” The true logical connection is this: “I am richer than you, therefore my property must exceed yours.” “I am more eloquent than you, therefore my style must surpass yours.” But you, in the end, consist neither in property nor in style.

chapters.title: Chapter 44
paragraphs: Does someone bathe hastily? Do not say that he bathes badly, but that he bathes hastily. Does someone drink a great deal of wine? Do not say that he drinks badly, but that he drinks a great deal. For unless you fully understand his motives, how should you know whether he acts badly? In this way you will not risk yielding to any appearances except those you fully comprehend.

chapters.title: Chapter 45
paragraphs: Never proclaim yourself a philosopher, nor make much talk about your principles among the ignorant; show them instead by your actions. At a banquet, do not speak of how people ought to eat, but eat as you ought. Remember that Socrates always avoided ostentation in the same way. When people came to him wishing to be introduced to philosophers, he took them and did so; so well did he bear being overlooked. So if ever, among the ignorant, there is some talk of philosophical principles, be silent for the most part. There is great danger in hastily bringing up what has not yet been digested. And if someone tells you that you know nothing, and you are not stung by it, then you may be sure that you have truly begun your work. For sheep do not hastily bring up the grass to show the shepherds how much they have eaten; they digest their food inwardly, and produce it outwardly in wool and milk. In the same way, do not make a display of your principles before the ignorant, but of the actions to which their digestion gives rise.

chapters.title: Chapter 46
paragraphs: When you have learned to nourish your body frugally, do not pride yourself on it; nor, if you drink only water, keep announcing on every occasion, “I drink water.” Consider first how much more frugal the poor are than we, and how much more patient under hardship. If at any time you wish to train yourself through exercise for labor and privation — for your own sake and not for the public — do not attempt great feats; when you are violently thirsty, simply rinse your mouth with water, and tell no one.

chapters.title: Chapter 47
paragraphs: The condition and mark of a vulgar person is that he never looks for help or harm from himself, but only from externals. The condition and mark of a philosopher is that he looks to himself for all help and all harm. The marks of one making progress are these: he censures no one, praises no one, blames no one, accuses no one; he says nothing of himself as being anyone or knowing anything. When he is in any instance hindered or restrained, he accuses himself. If he is praised, he smiles inwardly at the one praising him; if he is censured, he offers no defense. He goes about with the caution of a convalescent, careful not to disturb anything that is healing but not yet fully secure. He suppresses desire; he directs his aversion only toward those things that thwart the proper use of the will; he uses his energies moderately in every direction; if he appears stupid or ignorant, he does not mind. In a word, he watches over himself as over an enemy lying in ambush.

chapters.title: Chapter 48
paragraphs: When someone takes pride in being able to understand and interpret the works of Chrysippus, say to yourself: “Had Chrysippus not written obscurely, this man would have had nothing to be proud of. But what do I want? To understand nature and follow her. I ask, then, who interprets her; and when I hear that Chrysippus does, I turn to him. I do not understand his writings, so I seek someone to interpret them.” So far there is nothing to pride myself on. And when I find an interpreter, what remains is to put his teachings into practice. That alone is the valuable thing. But if I admire only the interpretation, I become nothing more than a grammarian instead of a philosopher — except that I am interpreting Chrysippus instead of Homer. So when someone asks me to read Chrysippus to him, I rather blush when I cannot show actions that harmonize with his discourse.

chapters.title: Chapter 49
paragraphs: Whatever rules you have adopted, abide by them as laws, as though it would be impious to break them; and pay no attention to what anyone says of you, for this, after all, is no concern of yours. How long, then, will you delay to require of yourself the noblest improvements, and in no instance to transgress the judgments of reason? You have received the philosophical principles with which you ought to be familiar, and you have been familiar with them. What other master, then, do you wait for, to excuse this delay in self-reformation? You are no longer a boy, but a grown man. If you remain negligent and slothful, and keep adding procrastination to procrastination, purpose to purpose, fixing day after day when you will attend to yourself, you will imperceptibly accomplish nothing, and you will live and die of a vulgar mind. This very moment, then, consider yourself worthy to live as a grown man, making progress. Let whatever appears best be to you an inviolable law. And if any instance of pain or pleasure, glory or disgrace, is set before you, remember that now is the contest, now the Olympiad arrives; it cannot be put off; and by one failure, one defeat, honor can be lost — or won. So Socrates became perfect, improving himself in everything, following reason alone. Although you are not yet a Socrates, you ought to live as one who seeks to be a Socrates.

chapters.title: Chapter 50
paragraphs: The first and most necessary topic in philosophy is the practical application of principles — for example, We ought not to lie. The second is that of demonstrations — for example, Why it is that we ought not to lie. The third gives strength and logical connection to the other two — for example, Why this is a demonstration. What is demonstration? What is a consequence? What is contradiction? What is truth? What is falsehood? The third point is needed on account of the second, and the second on account of the first. But the most necessary, and the one on which we should rest, is the first. We, however, do just the opposite. We spend all our time on the third point, lavishing all our diligence on it, and entirely neglect the first. So, while we lie, we are very ready to demonstrate that lying is wrong.
On every occasion we ought to have these maxims ready at hand:
Conduct me, Zeus, and you, O Destiny, / Wherever your decrees have fixed my lot. / I follow cheerfully; and, did I not, / Wicked and wretched, I must follow still.
Whoever yields properly to Fate is deemed / Wise among men, and knows the laws of Heaven.
And this third:
“O Crito, if this is what pleases the gods, so let it be.”
“Anytus and Meletus may kill me, but they cannot hurt me.”
